title: ‘Lilo & Scratch’: Disney Animation Blends 2D and 3D to Bring Back Stitch to the Big Screen in a New Short
full_text: × Nov 13, 2026 9:00am PT ‘Lilo & Scratch’: Disney Animation Blends 2D and 3D to Bring Back Stitch to the Big Screen in a New Short By Carole Horst Plus Icon Carole Horst Latest AI ‘Gods,’ Big-Budget Sci Fi, Star-Studded Genre Pics and More Generate Buzz at AFM 2 days ago AFM: First Look at Highland Film Group Thriller ‘The Black Demon: Atlantis’ Starring Jack Kesy (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago The ‘Air Bud Returns’ Team Hits AFM With Reenergized International Sales and More Family-Friendly Canine Adventures (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Walt Disney Animation The new animated short “Lilo & Scratch” immediately sets up audience expectations with its opening shot featuring a clip of the Three Stooges — expect comic hijinks, anarchy and cartoon destruction. For the first “Lilo & Stitch” project from Disney Animation since the original 2002 feature, and the first short from the unit in five years, directors Malcolm Pierce and Fawn Veerasunthorn ride the anarchy of the Stooges that lives in Stitch and introduce a new character, Scratch, a cute, cuddly kitten whose destructive forces rival the Lilo’s beloved blue “dog.” The short will unspool before Disney’s “Hexed,” which will be released Nov. 25. “Stitch is awesome,” says Pierce. “I feel like what I love is that he sort of lets his intrusive thoughts win, but he’s kind of a troublemaker too, which is really fun. So that was just super exciting, just to see what we can do that could put Stitch in a situation where he can make the most mischievous and troublemaking choices.” The plot of the short sees Lilo come home with a cute cat, which she calls Scratch, then leave the new pet in the care of Stitch (who’s watching the Three Stooges with glee). The cat quickly shows its true colors, creating trouble in ever-escalating comic situations that are laugh out loud funny and absurd. Related Stories 'Nobody Wants This' Renewed for Season 4 at Netflix Hollywood's Next Big Deal: Will Netflix Make an M&A Play for NBCU? Veerasunthorn is also a big Stitch fan, noting the 2002 film’s bold comedy and “the character’s deep desire to belong. It also came out when I was still in art school, so this film had made a big impression on me as an artist.” She adds that “when Jared Bush, [Walt Disney Animation Studios] chief creative officer, had this casual conversation with us — and I say casual because it happened in the hallway” to create a comedy-forward short “that showcases the fun of animation,” it was a no-brainer to go back to Lilo and Stitch. She says that she, Pierce and producer Nathan Curtis bounced around ideas and they narrowed the theme down to one question: Wouldn’t it be fun if chaotic stitch had to take care of a mysterious cute cat? Bush also wanted to play with new techniques for their animation pipeline. “The most exciting thing was to kind of merge these two worlds from Disney Animation, this old school Disney renaissance 2D aesthetic with our more modern CG pipeline,” says VFX supervisor Jeremy Sikorski. “We got a taste of what this would be on some of our other short form projects like ‘Paper Man’ and more recently, ‘Once Upon a Studio.’ So this felt like a real opportunity to somewhat officialize and push things even further to see where we could kind of take these aesthetics that the world has loved for so many years.” He adds: “We asked ourselves how could we create a production pipeline that no matter the artist’s chosen mediums, they could work in the project and work all together — quite often in the same exact frame — in a totally revolutionary and new way of working.” For the short, they studied the original feature and created a “toolset that would allow artists to blend their talents.” For example, a background could be hand-painted watercolor, but the Lilo and Stitch characters set against the background are 3D sculptures. They did an early test to see if their concept was going to work, using a hand-drawn Scratch and a CG Stitch holding a blaster in a sequence. “And the blaster he’s holding actually transitions from CG to hand drawn as Scratch eats it. When we looked at the finished results of this test, we were convinced we could do it, and we knew this was going to work, which is super exciting,” says Sikorski. Adds Veerasunthorn, “We wanted to give our artists an ability to choose their preferred medium to create a brand-new background for the short. So we actually do both. Some of these are digitally painted in Photoshop to look like watercolor, and some are actually hand painted on paper traditionally.” The six-minute short packs a lot of action and gags. “I think because Stitch is so popular, folks have an assumption of what Stitch is. He’s in merchandise everywhere. He’s he can be so familiar nowadays, so we really wanted to remind people of how you know hardcore he can be, how he can break stuff, and gets grumpy, and he’s got an edge to him, and so we really had fun just thinking about ‘What are all like the crazy things Stitch can do?’” says Pierce. Veerasunthorns adds: “We thought, who would be the worthy opponent of Stitch? They must meet each other at the same one-upping level. You know we always think Stitch would say, ‘I got this,’ and then Scratch would be like ‘Hold my beer, I got more.’ How do they kind of keep escalating the situation? And actually, the first cut of this reel was about 10 minutes because we had so many more jokes, and we had to narrow it down and say goodbye to some of our darlings.” A cat opponent would be a natural antagonist for Stitch, who’s still called Lilo’s “ugly blue dog.” Veerasunthorn said her initial design was more mysterious-looking and sort of weird, but they realized she had to be a lot cuter for audiences to embrace her. She also needed her own sound, which is where composers Haim Mazar and Grace Fisher came in. “She definitely has, like, a heavy metal voice, which is very unique to this short,” says Fisher. The duo had a lot of fun creating the music for the comedic action sequences — inspired by Carl Stalling and Tom and Jerry cartoons. The familiar had to blend with the new in the short. Says Mazar, “One of our biggest challenges was coming up with something that would feel fresh and contemporary, and at the same time, feel familiar, so that right from the first note you feel like, ‘I know this world’ and welcome to our ohana, so to speak. I think if I had to explain it, it was it was probably a combination of the style of the melodic material that we were we were going for something that would feel like it’s melodic and maybe even lyrical at times, but it also has a little sense of — I guess dare I say — pop music, and it it feels like a little bit of a fun ear worm.” Mazar adds that they recorded an orchestra, but also “small ensembles that had a lot of close miking and very tactile sounding shakers and and and all sorts of Hawaiian guitars, and I think producing it in a way that feels very contemporary, like a like a like a record that you would hear nowadays, and fusing that with the orchestra was what kind of gave it a little bit of a fresh taste.” Veerasunthorns adds that because the characters are mostly non-verbal, it’s really like paradise for animation. … the fact that we are able to get hand-drawn artists and CG animators working together is something that we’re super proud of, because we used to be like either or, and everyone just wanted to work on it.” Arnold Schwarzenegger Explains to Jimmy Kimmel Why He’s ‘Absolutely’ Still a Republican After the Blue ‘Tsunami’ Midterms Aly Muritiba Says It Was ‘Revolutionary’ to Centre Black Joy in Brazilian Musical ‘Funk’ Led by Rising Star Duda Santos ‘Kantara: A Legend,’ ‘The Kerala Story 2,’ Volker Schlondorff’s ‘Visitation’ Among 15 Films in Goa Festival International Competition Vampire Santa Claus Is Coming to Town in Ilja Rautsi’s Charades-Sold ‘Red Snow,’ Which Debuts Clip: ‘It’s a Gruesome Christmas Present’ (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Heartland’ Review: Jessica Chastain Rocks a Stetson and a Swagger for a Soapy Nashville Noir Aspyn Ovard on Her Divorce, Being in a Throuple and Joining ‘The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives’ Universe: ‘I Hope People Can Understand Me a Little Bit Better’ Loading comments...

title: Evil Moms: From ‘East of Eden’ to ‘Carrie,’ TV’s Latest Trope Is Honoring Women Who Choose Themselves
full_text: × Nov 13, 2026 9:00am PT Evil Moms: From ‘East of Eden’ to ‘Carrie,’ TV’s Latest Trope Is Honoring Women Who Choose Themselves By Aramide Tinubu Plus Icon Aramide Tinubu Latest Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan’s Heist Drama ’12 12 12′ Feels Like a Bad Video Game: TV Review 3 hours ago Netflix’s Genre-Bending YA Drama ‘The Body’ Is a Queer Y2K Extravaganza: TV Review 2 days ago ‘Wanted’ Broadway Review: Dazzling Cast Can’t Elevate the Musical’s Muted Narrative 5 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source COURTESY OF NETFLIX / SUZANNE TENNER/NETFLIX / Peacock / Courtesy of Prime / David Astorga Television has recently been preoccupied with evil moms, or at least that’s who they appear to be at first glance. In Zoe Kazan’s sweeping adaptation of John Steinbeck’s “ East of Eden ,” Lee (Hoon Lee), the Trask family’s domestic servant and surrogate father to the twin boys Aron (Joe Anders) and Cal (Joseph Zada), offers a poignant reflection. “There’s a beauty in the truth, even if it’s a dreadful beauty,” he says. Often, we evade or step around the facts. But dishonesty, no matter how innocent, is extremely harmful. The truth is that the world has rarely, if ever, been a safe space for women. To come of age in a patriarchal and violent society is a horrific thing. It corrodes the mind. It also forces girls and women to choose between two distinct paths. You either lean into male-centeredness or shun it entirely. Unfortunately, because patriarchy is a system that cannot be usurped, whether you lean toward it or try to burn it down, you will always be seen as monstrous by someone. Related Stories Netflix Hires Apple Alum Steve Wilson to Lead Podcast Content Acquisition Alex de la Iglesia on His Upcoming Chilean Shoot ‘The Misunderstanding’: ‘Reality Has Become My Parallel World’ Television programming typically works in conversation with popular culture. Currently, there is a lot to be said about motherhood, women’s experiences across time and what it truly means to be evil. Netflix’s “ Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story ” and “East of Eden,” Peacock’s “Friday the 13th” prequel “ Crystal Lake ,” Prime Video’s “ Carrie ” and Hulu’s comedic thriller “ Phony ” are distinct entities that all speak to one another. These are narratives centered on women reclaiming their stories from men who have only been able to view them in limited ways. These shows are all about women who have done horrendous things. However, their actions, despite how they’re presented on the surface, have not been without reason. In popular culture, men are depicted as barbarous, causing harm with impunity. Their behaviors are justified because, under patriarchy, men are poorly socialized and rely on women for empathy, care and comfort. As a result, when villainous men appear on screen in series like Ryan Murphy’s “Monster” franchise, Starz’s “Power” universe or HBO’s “Half Man,” they are senselessly volatile, nasty and murderous. This is not to suggest that women are immune to psychopathy. Yet their rates are far lower than men’s. Moreover, by living in a world not built for them, many women have learned to mask their most callous traits, making them unassuming and often, more lethal. When a woman is outwardly sinister, it typically shocks those around her. As Cathy Ames (Florence Pugh) reflects in “East of Eden,” “Evil is not always apparent at first glance; it can come cloaked in beauty or goodness or love.” Furthermore, when people learn these depraved women are mothers, it completely upends how the matriarchal role is viewed, making them all the more compelling. Florence Pugh in “East of Eden” COURTESY OF NETFLIX Perhaps it’s the nature of where we are in society, as female healthcare becomes increasingly sparse in certain parts of the country, as a rapist sits in the White House and as a generation of men seems intent on dragging women back in time to the 1950s. No matter the fixation, streamers, in particular, are turning their lens on several women determined to gain their agency by any means necessary. In “Monster: Lizzie Borden,” set in the late 19th century, Lizzie (Ella Beatty) is terrorized by her conniving stepmother, Abby (Rebecca Hall), whom she calls Mrs. Borden. Because of the confining nature of her role as a bored, bitter housewife (despite her privilege), Mrs. Borden revels in wickedness. With no recourse against her aloof, philandering husband, Andrew (Charlie Hunnam), she lashes out at the only people she can control: her staff and her naive, flighty stepdaughter. Wielding her cruelty for sport, the first two episodes of “Lizzie Borden” show Mrs. Borden throwing hot soup in her maid’s face, beating Lizzie and speaking to her harshly. However, the final straw before Lizzie swings the ax, ending Mrs. Borden’s life, comes when the older woman shoots up the girl’s beloved dovecote in a flurry of bloody feathers. Mrs. Borden likely always had a tinge of nastiness to her spirit, but being trapped in a marriage with no recourse to freedom exacerbated it. It’s no surprise, then, that when a monster raises you, you often become larger and more vicious than ever dreamed. Rebecca Hall and Ella Beatty in “Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story” SUZANNE TENNER/NETFLIX Mrs. Borden’s villainy likely stems from boredom and resentment. But some women are forced to emerge from something much more depraved. When “East of Eden” opens, audiences meet a bloodied and battered Cathy. She is on the brink of death as she drags herself onto the porch of brothers Adam (Christopher Abbott) and Charlie’s (Mike Faist) modest Connecticut home. Though Adam is immediately mesmerized by Cathy, Charlie, barely able to contain his fury, senses the darkness within her. Like Mrs. Borden, Cathy’s wickedness does not sprout from thin air. In Kazan’s narrative, she is sexually abused at age 5. This horrific incident forces Cathy to see the world in all of its depravity and the maddening horror of the people who let it fester in an effort to keep the peace. With absolute disdain for social norms and an understanding of the power and burden of her beauty, Cathy decides to carve her own path. She uses the men around her, including Adam, to obtain the one thing she’s striving for — financial independence. She does terrible things, but she is always honest about her intentions. She abandons her twin sons, telling Adam, “I don’t want them, I won’t change.” Later, when she sets her sights on Madame Faye (Martha Plimpton) to steal her brothel, she warns the older woman of her intentions before doing just that. Cathy is cold and calculated, but she is not overtly evil; she is unpunishable in a world intent on punishing women for much less. Linda Cardellini in “Crystal Lake” Peacock A half-century later in Peacock’s “Crystal Lake,” Pam Voorhees (Linda Cardellini) is grieving her dead son. Previously immersed in the joys and trials of motherhood, she is adrift without Jason (Callum Vinson). Yet, the world wounded her long before her son drowned. Her humiliation begins a decade earlier when her husband moves her from New York City to Texas for what she believes is advanced prenatal treatment. Following Jason’s birth, she learns they’ve both been experimented on for the sake of her husband’s career. Though she escapes and tries to put the horrible endeavor behind her, after Jason dies and her husband hunts her down, Pam lashes out in gruesome ways. Her wrath, like Lizzie’s, is not self–made — it is born out of the lie of female hysteria which festers under the stifling cloak of misogyny. Presently, America seems stuck in a state of appalling religious psychosis, a space Margaret White in “Carrie” knows all too well. Though she loves Carrie (Summer H. Howell), Margaret lets herself become a puppet of the patriarchy. Loyal to a male-centric theology, she terrorizes her only child, not even offering her the compassion of understanding her own body and menstrual cycle. What’s intriguing is that it’s clear Margaret feels trapped by her own religious beliefs, which is why, out of a desire to steer her own ship, she fashions herself an anti-bullying crusader while actively bullying and abusing Carrie. Instead of breaking the mold she’s been given, especially in the wake of her conspiracy theorist husband’s death, she chooses to work within it while manipulating and acting cruelly for her own gain. Summer H. Howell and Samantha Sloyan in “Carrie” Liane Hentscher/ Prime Finally, there is Ellen Cooke from “Phony” (Connie Britton). Though the show is told mostly from the perspective of Ellen’s teenage son, Sonny (Sam Nivola), the series showcases how deeply present and active maternal figures affect their children’s well-being and what happens when those children sense something is amiss. Though Ellen isn’t as openly chaotic and sinister as Mrs. Borden, Cathy, Pam or Margaret, she acts in unnerving ways, shattering the connection Sonny has spent a lifetime building with her. The horror then becomes when women aren’t behaving as society or even their children expect them to. Television is most interesting when characters are allowed to do outrageous things. When women operate outside of social norms, particularly mothers, it can be seen as horrific. The ladies depicted in these shows certainly have heinous moments. Yet, much of the terror we feel as viewers is because they choose themselves, even if it’s at the expense of their children. But perhaps what’s more evil is the fact that we live in a world where women haven’t been allowed to be self-serving. Should true freedom be widely granted to women, there would be little need for the nefarious deeds committed by the women in these shows. title: Unauthorized ‘Gilmore Girls’ Doc ‘Drink Coffee, Talk Fast’ Sets Release Date as Series Alum Scott Patterson Joins as Producer (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Nov 13, 2026 9:00am PT Unauthorized ‘Gilmore Girls’ Doc ‘Drink Coffee, Talk Fast’ Sets Release Date as Series Alum Scott Patterson Joins as Producer (EXCLUSIVE) By Jennifer Maas Plus Icon Jennifer Maas TV Business Writer @jmaasaronson Latest ‘Wolfenstein 3’ in Development at Xbox’s MachineGames 17 hours ago ‘Unlike Anything Else’: As ‘GTA 6’ Approaches, the Gaming Industry Braces the World for Its Pop Culture Takeover 20 hours ago More Than Half of Video Game Workers Laid Off Over the Past Two Years Are Still Unemployed, GDC Industry Report Finds 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ink On Paper Studios The “ Gilmore Girls ” documentary “Drink Coffee, Talk Fast” will be releasing on video-on-demand platforms next week with series alum Scott Patterson (who played the beloved Luke Danes) now on board as an executive producer and doc subject. Airing for seven seasons on The WB/CW from 2000-2007 with a one-season revival at Netflix in 2016, “Gilmore Girls” starred Lauren Graham and Alexis Bledel as iconic mother-and-daughter-duo Lorelai and Rory Gilmore. Related Stories ‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment’ Creators Break Down Its Shocking Finale Netflix Names Mattel Executive Roberto Stanichi as VP of Consumer Products and Experiences Per Ink On Paper Studios, the unauthorized documentary about the series will feature “all new, never-before-seen interviews with cast members, behind-the-scenes insights from the crew, stories from writers and directors, and heartfelt testimonials from fans whose lives were changed by the show.” Initially revealed as a Kickstarter project that hit its goal within its first 48 hours in September 2025, “Drink Coffee, Talk Fast” is now available to rent along with exclusive bonus content from the documentary-making process. The doc will be wildly available to stream for a fee on Apple, Google, and other major platforms on Tuesday, Nov. 17. “Drink Coffee, Talk Fast” is not affiliated with “Gilmore Girls” IP holder Warner Bros. Entertainment Inc. or the producers of “Gilmore Girls.” An authorized “Gilmore Girls” documentary is currently in the works at HBO Max with participation from creator Amy Sherman-Palladino alongside her husband, executive producer Daniel Palladino, and star Lauren Graham. Patterson’s participation in the “Gilmore Girls” doc is being announced ahead of the the film’s premiere at The Palace Theater in Los Angeles Friday as part of the Secret Movie Club and Los Angeles International Film Festival (LAIFF). Patterson will also be featured in the doc, alongside a number of new names just added to the cast list, in footage that was shot after the Kickstarter campaign ended. “Drink Coffee, Talk Fast” is directed by documentary filmmakers Meghna Balakumar and Kevin Konrad Hanna (“Clockwork Girl,” “Mike Mignola: Drawing Monsters”). Adam F. Goldberg is an executive producer. Jim Demonakos is a producer. “We couldn’t have been more excited to have Scott join us for this film,” Balakumar said. “He is so deeply connected to the ‘Gilmore Girls’ fandom, and we’re so glad we had the opportunity to capture that.” Along with Patterson (known for playing Lorelai Gilmore’s longtime will-they-won’t-they love Luke Danes), newly announced documentary participants include Lesli Linka Glatter (director), Susanne Daniels (former president of entertainment, The WB), Demi Adejuyigbe (co-host of the “Gilmore Guys” podcast), Rachel Kamerman (production designer), Mark Strasburg (first assistant camera) and Stephen Clancy (steadicam operator and director). These actors join the number of previously announced interviewees, including: Kelly Bishop (Emily Gilmore), Jared Padalecki (Dean Forester), Chad Michael Murray (Tristin Dugray), Keiko Agena (Lane Kim), Sally Struthers (Babette Dell), Liz Torres (Miss Patty), Emily Kuroda (Mrs. Kim), Rose Abdoo (Gypsy, Berta), Kathleen Wilhoite (Liz Danes), Michael Winters (Taylor Doose), Aris Alvarado (Caesar), Matt Jones (Morgan), Nick Holmes (Robert), Grant Lee Phillips (the town troubadour), George Anthony Bell (Professor Bell), Shelly Cole (Madeline Lynn), Vanessa Marano (April Nardini) and Olivia Hack (Tana Schrick) as well as director Jamie Babbit, writer and producer Stan Zimmerman, costumer Valerie Campbell, casting directors Jami Rudofsky and Mara Casey, and “Gilmore Guys” podcast co-host Kevin T Porter. title: ‘Russell Brand: Open Secret’ Director Says Finding Contributors Wasn’t Easy: ‘There’s Been a Landscape of Fear’
full_text: × Nov 13, 2026 8:56am PT ‘Russell Brand: Open Secret’ Director Says Finding Contributors Wasn’t Easy: ‘There’s Been a Landscape of Fear’ By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest David Walliams Being Investigated for ‘Serious Sexual Offences’ by Police 33 minutes ago ‘Russell Brand: Open Secret’: Netflix Doc Reveals His ‘Jokes’ About Rape, Making a Girlfriend ‘Brush Her Teeth Until They Bled’ and More 1 hour ago Kaylee Hottle’s Sister Will Step in to Complete ‘Godzilla’ Actor’s Last Movie After Her Death at 18 Years Old 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images It didn’t take Netflix long to deliver what might be the definitive documentary about the rise and fall of Russell Brand , the former comedian who was sentenced this week to ten and a half years in prison after being convicted of rape and sexual assault. “Russell Brand: Open Secret,” which includes testimony from ex-partners and fellow comedians , charts not only Brand’s career but also the media climate than enabled him to flourish despite effective hiding in plain sight. Related Stories Netflix U.K. Layoffs Hit Up to 3% of London HQ, Production VP Anna Mallett Exits Netflix Names Mattel Executive Roberto Stanichi as VP of Consumer Products and Experiences Hours after the doc debuted on Netflix, director Olivia Isaacs (“The Other Mrs Jordan: Catching the Ultimate Swindler”) sat down with Variety to discuss the process of making the film while his trial was looming, whether it was easy to find contributors and if she’s worried about backlash. When did you start working on this? November 2023, so two months after the allegations broke. This was pre-police investigation. It was very early days, so our whole focus was we’ve got this man, this huge celebrity, and now these allegations. Is there a wider, broader piece to be done? He’s a big Noughties figure. We wanted to look at the cultural backdrop. We weren’t sure what was going to happen to him, so it was a quite interesting moment. Once he’s charged, the media in the U.K. isn’t allowed to publish or broadcast anything that could prejudice the trial. How did that impact your process? We were never going to rush the process anyway. So we were still very much in our first throes of production at that point, and the moment they announced an investigation, we thought “We do not want to impact any future trial.” We were acutely aware that there might be charges any minute, and then after the charges we didn’t know the timeframes but there would be a trial. So I think we were just always trying to be responsible filmmakers and mitigate against that. The documentary examines the course of Brand’s career but doesn’t go deep into the recent criminal court case. Did you consider bringing more of the case into it? There was a discussion: do we follow it? But I think we felt like we had a bigger message and bigger broader understanding to get out there…. and I think we wanted to add our voice in within this moment rather than wait. Netflix have released the doc just over a week after Brand was convicted. What would have happened if he had been acquitted of all the charges? Was there a different cut ready to go? I think we are very aware that legally if someone’s found innocent then you are in a different legal scenario … that does make it more difficult to publish. If he’d gotten let off, we potentially were looking at maybe we’d have to do a reversion down the line. But then we thought, what’s our story? You know, what are we adding to this culturally at that point? We never knew what was going to happen but we made the film with the mindset of “This would likely go out with some sort of guilty verdict” but there was a lot hinging on what that might look like and then our duty of care to the people within the film. How ready was it by the time the verdict came in? It was more or less 99.9% ready. And then we had the end cards, we wanted to put the sentencing and things in. There were a couple of tiny things that we had to double check legally. How easy was it to find contributors? As we all know, there’s been a landscape of fear. It’s been a litigious minefield for many years, reporting anything on Brand. So despite some people coming forward, everyone was still in that mindset. It wasn’t definitely easy. “Easy” would never be the word I’d use for this. It took a lot of building trust and a lot of conversations, and even then, many people didn’t feel comfortable. There were a lot of nerves and fear, and they’d been in their minds silenced up until now, or had signed NDAs, or you know, there were lots of complexities to it. So it was a slow process of speaking to as many people as possible. Was there anyone in particular that you’d hoped to speak to that you couldn’t get for this? We were open-minded and led by the access and who was willing to speak. I mean, of course, for me as a filmmaker, I’d always like to hold people to account as well and hear from that side and unfortunately those people did not want to sit in front of the camera and take accountability. I’d say there’s many people from that side that we would have liked to [speak to] or wished that they just taken that moment to sort of acknowledge it and, as I say, take accountability. I think that is probably the most lacking voice out there at the moment, never mind the film. You mean the people around him who enabled him and protected him? Exactly. You know, agents, exec producers, people who are minding the talent. People giving him the work. One thing the documentary shows really clearly is how Brand would morph into whatever persona was the most expedient, particularly when he moved into political influencing, first on the left and then the right. How did you approach that? He’s had all these different personas and guises and so that was always my first thought, aside from the allegations, [that was] fascinating to me. And then, of course, because we were [making it] over three years, you were able to sort of chart this backlash to the Me Too movement that we were acutely living in and still are living in, and the development of the “manosphere” and this far-right conspiracy space, and Russell turning up into that space. So for me, I was fascinated that his story takes us into the story of now and the [current political] “dividedness,” and it wasn’t necessarily a sensitive space to exist in, but just interesting, I guess. I’ve heard Netflix are good at providing support to documentary-makers covering subjects with very passionate fan bases. Have they been supportive to you given Brand’s fanbase (some of whom turned up to court to support him) can be very vocal? I think there was always a sense from day dot the duty of care around everyone off camera as well, and supporting everyone through that. I think the industry’s got better at doing that too. We had trauma-informed training early on, both for us and for the contributors that we knew we’d be speaking to, as well as other bits of training just around the management of what we might be listening to and watching for such a long period of time, so it felt like there was a lot of support in general, not necessarily, you know, acutely around any backlash and things. But Netflix are amazing at providing online security guidance and support. They’ve got teams that check out your profile online and make sure that you’re not accidentally revealing your address anywhere and things like that. So it felt like there was a nice web of support around myself and the whole team. But I don’t think we’ve [had] any scaremongering to worry too much about the fans. There’s always going to be people online. It’s already dividing everyone’s opinion on socials. title: Taylor Swift to Perform at the 2026 CMA Awards
full_text: × Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All November 13, 2026 8:34am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Taylor Swift attends the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards at Peacock Theater on Sept. 27. Frazer Harrison/Getty Images Taylor Swift is making a big return to the CMA Awards . The superstar singer-songwriter, who’d indicated when nominations were announced that she’d attend the country music awards show, is not only attending but performing at the 2026 CMA Awards . Swift previously appeared at the ceremony, known as Country Music’s Biggest Night, a decade ago and last performed there 13 years ago. Swift is a two-time CMA Entertainer of the Year, becoming the youngest ever winner of that honor in 2009, and in 2013 received the Pinnacle Award. She’s nominated this year for single of the year for her Toy Story 5 song “I Knew It, I Knew You,” which is seen as a top contender for a song of the year Oscar nomination. Related Stories TV How to Stream the 2026 Latin Grammys Online Movies You Can't See Everything: The Sneaky Problem With the Elizabeth Holmes Documentary Swift’s performance at the CMA Awards will take place two days after the 2026 Grammy nominations are announced, where Swift is expected to be a top contender both for “I Knew It, I Knew You” and The Life of a Showgirl , which was released after the end of Grammys eligibility last year. Swift was also recently announced as the recipient of The Hollywood Reporter ‘s prestigious Sherry Lansing Leadership Award , which she’ll accept at THR ‘s 2026 Women in Entertainment gala. “I Knew It, I Knew You” marks a return to Swift’s country music roots after a number of pop albums in recent years. So it’s fitting she’s also returning to the CMA Awards for this nomination. She first attended the CMA Awards in 2006 and performed “Red” with Vince Gill and Alison Krauss at the 2013 CMA Awards. In 2016, her last appearance at the CMA Awards, she presented Garth Brooks with his Entertainer of the Year honor. When this year’s CMA Awards nominations were announced, Swift posted to her Instagram Stories , “LOOKS LIKE I HAVEN’T YEE’D MY LAST HAW THANK YOU CMA!!!! See you there Nov. 18 🤠.” The 60th annual CMA Awards will be hosted by Lainey Wilson for the third year in a row. The awards show will air live from Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena on Wednesday, Nov. 18 at 8 p.m. ET on ABC and Disney+ and will be available to stream the next day on Hulu. THR

title: Russell Brand Accused of Predatory Behavior by Several More Women: “I Begged Him to Stop”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All November 13, 2026 8:31am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Russell Brand during his Southwark Crown Court trial. Courtesy of Getty Convicted rapist Russell Brand is facing allegations of sexual misconduct from at least six more women in a new report from The Times and Netflix’s Russell Brand: Open Secret documentary. The disgraced comedian and actor is behind bars after being sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison on Monday. He was found guilty of one rape and three sexual assaults, and cleared on three other counts, in a landmark trial. The Hollywood Reporter has taken a deep dive into the years-long work to expose Brand as a sexual predator and bring him to justice. Related Stories Movies 'One Sweet Hour': One Aging Elvis Impersonator. One Monk. Two Estranged Irish Brothers Facing Trauma. Movies How 'Red Ink' Pulled Off a Single-Take, 1940s Vampire Newsroom Thriller Upon his sentencing, the Met Police had confirmed Brand was under investigation for two more alleged rapes. And then on Thursday, The Times revealed that he has been accused of predatory behavior and misconduct by another six women. This report has come from the two journalists who led the 2023 joint investigation into Brand by The Sunday Times and Channel 4’s Dispatches , which helped other victims of his decide to speak up and, ultimately, press criminal charges. From Charlotte Wace and Rosamund Urwin, the investigation includes an accusation that Brand had sex with a woman without her consent, then apologized afterwards. Another woman said that he continued having sex with her after she asked him to stop because he was hurting her. She says he later told her: “Tonight was consensual. Nobody did anything they didn’t want to do.” The Times added that these allegations “could not be reported until the criminal case against the former comedian and actor ended, to avoid prejudicing proceedings.” Wace and Urwin wrote that his lawyer said he would consider “injunctive relief” and demanded further time to respond, but the deadline eventually passed with no response — “despite prompts.” Brand maintained through his trial that all of his interactions were consensual. Wace and Urwin spoke to a woman called Vicky, who met Brand multiple times for consensual sex. On their final meeting, she says he initiated intimacy without any warning. “My body wasn’t ready for this and it was painful,” Vicky told The Times . “An uneasy wave hits me and I’m scared. And I say, ‘It’s painful,’ and he doesn’t stop. And then it gets worse and it’s really painful. And I say, ‘Stop,’ and he doesn’t stop.” She said: “It was like… he wasn’t present.” Another woman, called Zoe, said during their 2013 encounter — after Brand had split from pop star Katy Perry — he “grabbed me and manhandled me around a little bit and he put his hand on my throat. […] And then he shoved his other hand down my trousers and penetrated me with his finger.” She told The Times she froze. “I didn’t resist. I just sort of let it happen.” The final allegation from The Times ‘ latest piece of investigative work is from 2015 — when Brand was in a relationship with his now-wife and mother of his children, Laura, who accompanied him every day to court. She told the jury that Brand is a “caring and kind” person and a “wonderful father” to their three children. Louise, then in her late 20s, worked at a London venue that Brand frequented. One day, a woman approached Louise and asked where he was. “I thought it was just another obsessive fan… She told me she was his girlfriend, but others had said that too.” It was Laura Gallacher, who had dated Brand briefly in 2007 when she was 19 and he was 31. They rekindled their relationship in 2015. Louise said on one occasion, one of Brand’s staff told her, “‘Russell wants you,'” and that he was in the disabled toilets. Brand tried to “entice her” to come to the lavatory door, and had turned the lights off when she arrived. When Brand claimed he needed toilet paper, she went to hand it to him and he grabbed her. “It was halfway up my forearm, and I tried to get away. When I stepped back, I realized his [member of staff] was standing right behind me,” she recalls. She feared Brand would sexually assault her and managed to slip away. She went into the next room and cried, because “I felt like a piece of meat.” Both Wace and Urwin contributed to Netflix’s Friday release, Russell Brand: Open Secret , which also included allegations against the convicted sex offender. The film described the experience of an ex-girlfriend of his, under the pseudonym Emily. She said she “literally begged” Brand to stop after he refused to wear a condom during sex. “I said to him, ‘No, Russell, please, let’s just use protection,'” said an actress playing Emily in the film. “I kept saying ‘No’. I said, ‘Stop Russell, stop, please don’t, please.’ […] I literally begged him. I tried to kick him off, I tried to draw my knees back, to kick him in his belly, but he was too strong for me.” She says he “just pinned my hands back behind my head” before forcing himself on her. Brand is likely to serve around seven years of his prison sentence. Questions have been raised across the industry about how he was able to evade punishment for as long as he did. On Tuesday, another of his ex-girlfriends, Jemima Goldsmith, accused Brand of “violence, coercive control and abuse” while they were together. THR

title: Stephen King Almost Threw ‘Carrie’ in the Trash. Then It Changed Everything
full_text: × Skip to main content Sissy Spacek in 1976’s 'Carrie.' Courtesy Everett Collection In the early 1970s, Stephen King was a struggling and frustrated English teacher in Maine with a wife, two small children and a stack of bills that seemed to be growing much faster than his literary career. During the day, he taught teenagers at Hampden Academy. At night, he’d pound out short stories and quickie tales of terror for lower-tier skin magazines like Cavalier and Adam . The pay wasn’t much, but it kept the lights on … barely. “Two hundred dollars,” says King of his typical fee at the time. “Once in a while, it was $500. That was a huge payday. That bought a lot of groceries.” Things were so tight that the Kings didn’t even have a telephone. Related Stories TV Streaming Ratings Take on a Halloween Vibe With 'Crystal Lake,' 'Carrie' TV Streaming Ratings: 'Carrie' Has a Bloody Good Opening Week Then, in 1972, King began tinkering with an idea about a painfully awkward teenage girl who is mercilessly bullied by her classmates and terrorized at home by her religiously fanatical mother. When the girl discovers that she possesses telekinetic powers, she finally has a way to strike back. The story would reach its cathartic crescendo at her high school prom, where a horrifically cruel prank involving a bucket of pig’s blood turns what should have been the best night of her young life into an apocalyptic bloodbath. Her name was Carrie White. Although he had no way of knowing it at the time, the book he had just begun writing would change the course of his life. And not just his. The 1976 movie adaptation of Carrie would turn Sissy Spacek into a bona fide star, give Brian De Palma his first box office hit and pull off something scary movies almost never did, then or now: crash the Oscars. It would also mark the beginning of one of the most prolific — and lucrative — pipelines in movie history, with King’s stories adapted for the screen more than 60 times. Fifty years, several remakes, a notorious Broadway musical and one brand-new Prime Video series later, Carrie White’s bloody fingerprints are still everywhere you look. The inspiration for the novel that would become Carrie came from several places. Years earlier, while working as a school janitor, King had cleaned the girls’ locker room and noticed the sanitary napkin dispensers mounted on the walls. He began imagining a teenage girl experiencing her first period in the shower with no understanding of what was happening to her while her classmates responded with ridicule. He combined that image with his interest in telekinesis and his memories of two girls he’d known growing up who had been treated as social pariahs. “I wasn’t bullied,” King says. “I think that every kid feels a little bit bullied in school, but I had less of it than others.” The girls, however, weren’t as fortunate. “They were savagely bullied about their clothes, about their hair, just about their lack of social graces. They were country kids and they were really treated poorly.” What stuck with King was the impossibility of escaping the roles that high school had assigned them. Even when the girls tried to improve their appearance, their tormentors wouldn’t let them. “If they tried to wear new clothes or something like that after Christmas, they were bullied twice as hard,” he says. “Nobody wanted to let them out of the box.” That heartbreaking observation would become the emotional foundation of Carrie . Sometimes the only way out is to burn the whole place down. Carrie’s most powerful moment isn’t the prom night massacre; it’s the expression on Carrie’s face when she realizes she’s been crowned prom queen and believes, for perhaps the first time in her life, that she belongs. Then the blood falls. United Artists/Getty Images John Travolta, who plays a mean-girl boyfriend, combs the locks of his “stunt image.” Bettmann/Getty Images At first, King envisioned the story as another quick sale to Cavalier , which he calls his “go-to magazine” at the time. “I thought to myself, ‘Here’s an idea for a story: a girl who gets her first period and she’s telekinetic and she just gets back at these girls.’ ” But almost immediately, he ran into problems. For one thing, he wasn’t convinced he knew enough about the female experience to make the opening believable. “I didn’t know anything about girls’ locker rooms,” he says, beginning to laugh. “I didn’t know if there were coin-op machines for the napkins. I didn’t even know what the napkins were, for God’s sake.” Worse, the story was already growing beyond the magazine’s usual word count, and King feared it would end up being too long for a short story and too short for a novel. So he crumpled up the pages and threw them in the wastebasket. That might have been the end of Carrie White, except that King’s wife, Tabitha, discovered the discarded manuscript, read it and recognized something that her husband hadn’t. “Tabby fished it out and said, ‘You know, this is really good, so push on with it,’ ” King recalls. He did, and over the next three months, the little story he had abandoned grew into his first publishable novel. Fifty years later, when asked how often he has thanked his wife for retrieving those pages, King doesn’t even pause to think it over: “A lot.” King’s manuscript eventually landed on the desk of Bill Thompson, an editor at Doubleday who had already read several of King’s earlier, rejected novels. Thompson saw something in Carrie and invited the wannabe author to New York. King could barely afford the trip. His grandmother- in-law gave him the cash for a Greyhound ticket, and he traveled overnight from Maine, with no money for a hotel. Thompson took him to lunch, where several gin and tonics were consumed on the publisher’s dime. “I got pretty much blitzed,” King remembers. Afterward, he became hopelessly lost walking back to the Port Authority bus terminal. When he finally got home, Tabitha asked how the meeting had gone. “I think they might publish the book,” he told her. In 1973, Doubleday bought Carrie for $2,500. The news arrived by telegram because the Kings still didn’t have a phone. Tabitha received the message through Western Union and had her husband paged to the principal’s office over the school loudspeaker. King immediately imagined two possibilities: Either one of his children had been hurt or he’d sold the book. He still has the telegram, framed on the wall of his office in the much nicer house in Maine he now calls home, bearing Thompson’s wonderfully prophetic message: “The future lies ahead.” Carrie was published on April 5, 1974, with a modest first printing of 30,000 copies. It wasn’t an immediate sensation in hardcover (it sold about 13,000 copies), but critics were intrigued by the newcomer. The New York Times praised the novel’s assurance and imagination, recognizing that its mixture of supernatural terror and teenage cruelty marked the arrival of a distinctive voice. King, however, felt that Doubleday was too consumed with another one of its titles — Peter Benchley’s Jaws — to promote his book. A tale of two Carries on the key art in 1976. Courtesy Everett Collection Benchley presumably got a much bigger advance as well — King’s $2,500 was barely enough to splurge on a new Pinto. He didn’t exactly rake in a fortune when he sold the film rights, either. Veteran producer Paul Monash, whose credits included Peyton Place and Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid , offered a whopping $500 for the story rights. “And Doubleday got half of that,” says King. “So, $250. Big whoop. I could have made more from one of the Cavalier stories.” He took the offer anyway. Luckily, after the hardcover release there was a windfall when a New American Library editor fell in love with Carrie ‘s story and ponied up $400,000 for the paperback rights. Again, Doubleday got half, but it was enough for King to quit teaching and start writing full time. He also used a chunk of the money to help his mother, who was still working even though she was suffering from cancer. “I went to the place where she worked and I said, ‘You’re done,’ ” King recalls. “She cried. That was a great, great moment.” The film was set up at United Artists with a budget of $1.8 million — a modest figure even by the standards of the mid-1970s. And the director the studio landed on was then-35-year-old Brian De Palma, the New Hollywood movie brat who’d helmed the Hitchcockian 1972 thriller Sisters and the deliriously bonkers 1974 rock-horror musical Phantom of the Paradise . De Palma’s reputation was that of a dazzling visual stylist with a sweet tooth for split-screen trickery, daredevil camerawork and sexual provocation. The director’s drawn-out suspense sequences seemed to delight in torturing the audience. Still, for the most part, box office success had largely eluded him. De Palma immediately recognized Carrie ‘s potential and thought that it might lead to the commercial breakthrough that Jaws had recently given his pal Steven Spielberg. For his part, King was thrilled with the choice. He’d seen Sisters and picked up on a simpatico sensibility. The studio tapped Lawrence D. Cohen, a relative unknown, to adapt King’s novel. Cohen streamlined the book, including its climax. In the novel, Carrie devastates much of her hometown after the prom. But in the movie, the destruction is largely confined to the school gymnasium and back at her house, where she finally confronts her overbearing zealot mother. The adaptation was less sprawling and more intimate. When it came time to cast the film, De Palma and his friend George Lucas (who was looking for up-and-coming talent for his own in-the-works project, which he was calling Star Wars ) decided to pool resources and hold auditions for both films simultaneously. “George and I were both looking for young actors at the same time, so we held our casting sessions together,” De Palma once told me. “We both really wanted Amy Irving. George wanted her for Princess Leia.” William Katt, who eventually snagged the role of Carrie’s handsome prom date, was also considered for Luke Skywalker. The two movies couldn’t have been more different, but for a brief moment, they existed in the same galaxy. De Palma would eventually cast Irving as Sue Snell, the sympathetic classmate who tries to make amends for Carrie’s humiliation. Nancy Allen played Chris Hargensen, the spoiled, vindictive teenager who orchestrates the prom night prank. John Travolta, already familiar to television audiences as Vinnie Barbarino on Welcome Back, Kotter , played her dim-witted boyfriend. For the part of Carrie’s mother, De Palma recruited Piper Laurie, an Oscar nominee for 1961’s The Hustler who had spent much of the intervening period away from Hollywood. Laurie would approach her character’s religious hysteria with an almost operatic intensity. P.J. Soles (left) and Nancy Allen (right) as the mean girls. Says Stephen King about two young women he knew growing up: “They were savagely bullied about their clothes, about their hair, about their lack of social graces. They were country kids and they were really treated poorly.” Courtesy Everett Collection Brian De Palma during production. The director was known at the time for his dazzling visual style with a sweet tooth for split-screen trickery and daredevil camerawork. Marv Newton/MPTVImages.com The crucial role, however, remained unfilled. Maybe because it seemed unfillable. Sissy Spacek, a 26-year-old Texan who looked at least 10 years younger, had made an indelible impression as a teenage runaway opposite Martin Sheen in Terrence Malick’s Badlands in 1973, but she was hardly a household name. Her husband, though, production designer Jack Fisk, was working on Carrie and encouraged her to audition for the role. Spacek was supposed to shoot a television commercial on the weekend that De Palma asked her to come in, but she canceled it and showed up for her screen test instead. Spacek arrived looking as though she’d been dragged through the worst day of her life. She had rubbed Vaseline into her hair and wore an old sailor-style dress her mother had made when she was in seventh grade. Rather than try to make herself attractive, she transformed herself into someone almost painfully uncomfortable in her own skin. De Palma was blown away. Principal photography began in March 1976, with a 50-day schedule and a budget that left little room beyond the barest necessities. The production used an abandoned school in Hermosa Beach for many of its exteriors, while Fisk constructed the gymnasium on a Hollywood soundstage so it could be destroyed during the film’s climax: The sequence of slow-building, screw-tightening suspense set during Carrie’s high school prom — drenched in pig’s blood and supernatural mayhem — is arguably the greatest Hitchcock scene that Hitchcock never directed. When Carrie opened on Nov. 3, 1976, critics were surprisingly divided on the question of whether De Palma had made a brilliant horror movie or just an exceedingly well-made exploitation picture. In The New York Times , Vincent Canby sniffed at the film’s excesses, arguing that De Palma had encouraged his actors to push their performances beyond plausibility. Yet even Canby couldn’t resist the film’s leading lady. “The marvel, though, is Sissy Spacek,” he wrote, acknowledging that despite the heightened emotions, she made Carrie’s suffering genuinely moving. But others, like the Chicago Sun-Times ‘ Roger Ebert, were more enthusiastic. Ebert called the film “an absolutely spellbinding horror movie.” Amy Irving as the empathetic Sue Snell in Carrie. MPTVImages.com Audiences sided with Ebert. Carrie earned $33.8 million at the domestic box office — an impressive return on its $1.8 million budget. It marked De Palma’s first real commercial success. It also earned two Academy Award nominations, for Spacek as best actress and Laurie as best supporting actress, an unusual achievement for a horror movie in any era. As for King, he remembers seeing the film for the first time at a preview screening in Boston. He and Tabitha drove down from Maine to an inner-city theater, where Carrie was playing on a double bill with Norman … Is That You? , a comedy starring Redd Foxx. King recalls the audience being almost entirely Black, and he initially worried that the crowd might have little interest in his story about a white teenage girl’s traumatic adolescence. “I thought to myself, ‘Man, this audience is not going to care about this little white girl with her menstrual problems,’ ” he says. But as the film unspooled, the crowd became increasingly animated, shouting at the screen and really dialing into the film’s white-knuckle suspense. Then came the final scene. Sitting behind King were two men the size of football players. When Carrie’s hand suddenly burst through the grave, both shrieked and grabbed each other in terror. King recalls one of the men saying, “That’s it, that’s it. She ain’t never gonna be right.” That was when King knew the movie worked. “I thought to myself, ‘Well, we got a hit.’ “ When asked why Carrie still endures, King suspects it’s the primal satisfaction of watching an underdog get payback. “I think that it has something to do with the bullied child striking back,” he says. But the movie’s power is more complicated than just simple revenge. De Palma understood that the audience had to love Carrie before it could fear her. The movie’s most powerful moment isn’t the prom night massacre or even the final hand reaching from beyond the grave. It’s the expression on Spacek’s face when she realizes she’s been crowned prom queen and believes, for perhaps the first time in her life, that she belongs. For that one brief, beautiful moment, anything and everything seems possible. Then the blood falls, and the dream dies. And half a century later, we still can’t look away. title: David Walliams Under Investigation by U.K. Police Over Alleged “Serious Sexual Offenses”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All November 13, 2026 8:29am Add us as a Google Preferred Source David Walliams Courtesy of Getty David Walliams , the BAFTA-winning comedian and bestselling children’s author, is under investigation by London’s Metropolitan Police over “alleged serious sexual offenses.” BBC News has reported that the Met investigation is separate from the bombshell accusations Walliams faces in a joint report by ITV News and The Guardian released this week. The Met said it had “received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s… Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers,” the statement added. Related Stories Movies From Sandworms to 007: Joe Walker on 'Dune: Part Three,' Villeneuve, McQueen and Bond Movies 'One Sweet Hour': One Aging Elvis Impersonator. One Monk. Two Estranged Irish Brothers Facing Trauma. Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney urged anyone who has been a victim of a sexual offence to “come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.” He continued: “We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process.” Tuesday’s report detailed accusations of sexual assault and grooming by several women, some of whom allege they were as young as 15 when the interactions took place. Walliams, best known for roles in Little Britain , Come Fly With Me and as a judge on Britain’s Got Talent , had sought an injunction to prevent the two news organizations from publishing his identity, over fears that he would be “highly likely” to kill himself. He maintained that the suicide risk is not attributed to any wrongdoing but to what his lawyers described as “trial by media.” His lawyers have said that Walliams has already tried to take his own life twice. The injunction request was later rejected by a High Court judge, after which the British press has been free to publish Walliams’ identity. He vehemently denied the allegations and told ITV News and The Guardian: “I am not a sexual predator… I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me. […] Looking back, I realize that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with. I realize I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did.” The Hollywood Reporter reached out to his reps for comment this week and have not yet heard back. The claims surrounding Walliams have dominated the British media this week. One woman, Alex, says she was contacted by Walliams when she was 15 and he was 32, after meeting him at a Little Britain fan event. They began speaking on the phone and when she turned 17, Alex says, they were having sex. Multiple women accused Walliams of abusing his power and position to prey on them for sex. The majority claim to be over 18 when the encounters took place, but “several sources” also described inappropriate behavior toward young women on the set of Britain’s Got Talent and at his former publisher, HarperCollins. The company dropped him as a client last December amid claims of misconduct, which he denied at the time. Walliams is one of the country’s best-selling authors, having sold over 50 to 60 million copies of his books worldwide, with Gangsta Granny , Mr. Stink and The Boy in the Dress among his most famous. In response to Tuesday’s news, the BBC confirmed it would be removing some of its Walliams content, including episodes of Little Britain , from its streaming service iPlayer. Walliams was also dropped by his literary agent, the Independent Talent Group, and suspended by the Labour Party. Fremantle U.K., producers of Britain’s Got Talent — where Walliams is accused of sending inappropriate messages to young runners during filming — said the company is “disturbed and concerned” by the claims that have come to light. A spokesperson said to THR : “During his time on the show and in the intervening period, no complaint was ever made regarding [Walliams’] behaviour to Fremantle U.K. […] If anyone feels they have been the subject of any impropriety or wrongdoing by anyone on any Fremantle or associated labels’ productions, we encourage them to come forward. … We will treat any complaints seriously. Protecting the welfare of our employees, freelancers, contributors and fans has always been and absolutely remains paramount for the company.” THR

title: Johnny Depp’s ‘Ebenezer’ Unearths $1.5M in Box Office Previews
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All November 13, 2026 8:23am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Tramell Tillman (left) and Johnny Depp in 'Ebenezer.' Paramount Pictures Johnny Depp ‘s push for a career comeback is underway at the box office with the holiday-themed ghost story Ebenezer . Paramount Pictures releases Ebenezer in more than 3,500 North American theaters on Friday, with the movie grossing $1.5 million from Thursday previews. The studio projects director Ti West’s spooky adaptation of Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol to collect $20 million domestically and add another $20 million internationally from 63 worldwide markets. Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley and Ian McKellen round out the cast for the $38 million-budgeted feature that stars Depp as the miserly Ebenezer Scrooge. Ebenezer marks Depp’s return to studio fare following negative headlines surrounding his and ex-wife Amber Heard ‘s messy 2022 defamation trial and abuse allegations that Depp has denied. His most recent studio release was 2018’s Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald , as Warner Bros. dropped him from that franchise two years later after the actor lost a libel suit against the publisher of The Sun . The film has divided critics, as it holds a 52 percent approval from critics on Rotten Tomatoes. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter , critic Frank Scheck declares that Ebenezer “fulfills its ostensible goal of restoring the actor to A-list status.” Another major release is Amazon MGM Studios’ How to Rob a Bank , hitting 2,810 domestic theaters. Filmmaker David Leitch’s heist movie nabbed $900,000 in previews and is expected to launch in the high single digits in North America against a $40 million budget. Anna Sawai and Nicholas Hoult in How to Rob a Bank . Sony Pictures released Ghost Soldier in 2,558 North American locations on Wednesday, with director William Eubank’s action movie grossing $3.1 million over the two days, including Tuesday previews. title: Christian Cousins, Young Actor in ‘Knots Landing’ and ‘Kindergarten Cop,’ Dies at 43
full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All November 13, 2026 8:18am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Christian Cousins (left) and Joseph Cousins in 1989. Lorimar Television / Courtesy Everett Collection Christian Cousins, who with his identical twin brother shared roles as youngsters on the CBS primetime soap Knots Landing and in the Arnold Schwarzenegger film Kindergarten Cop , has died. He was 43. Cousins died Oct. 20 after a battle with liver disease, his half-brother Jonas Roeser announced on Instagram. “He was a character, full of passion and energy, with big stories and even bigger dreams,” he wrote. Christian and twin brother Joseph were not yet 4 when they first appeared on Knots Landing as Bobby Ewing during the show’s ninth season in 1987, and they wound up on 57 episodes through 1992. Related Stories TV Michael John Roberts, Animator and 'BoJack Horseman' and 'TripTank' Director, Dies at 48 TV Dan Hicks, NBC Sports Play-by-Play Legend, Dies at 64 Bobby, who had a twin sister, Betsy, was named by Joan Van Ark’s Valene Ewing after the character played by Patrick Duffy on Dallas was run over by a car driven by Morgan Brittany’s Katherine Wentworth. ( Knots Landing was a spinoff of Dallas , and producers there were fond of series crossovers and piggybacking off its Lorimar sibling.) In Kindergarten Cop (1990), directed by Ivan Reitman, Christian and Joseph portrayed Dominic, one of the students taught by Schwarzenegger’s John Kimble, an L.A. detective working undercover at an elementary school. Dominic’s mom is played by Penelope Ann Miller, and he winds up as a hostage. Christian Michail Cousins and Joseph were born on March 17, 1983, and raised in Orange County, California. After embarking on Knots Landing — their character was introduced on a November 1984 episode in which Val gives birth to Bobby and Betsy and then they’re kidnapped, resulting in a season-long storyline — Christian and Joseph shared roles on episodes of Father Dowling Mysteries , Eerie, Indiana and Intruders and in Critters 3 (1991). They played twins named Hope and Faith on a 1988 episode of Highway to Heaven and brothers named Bradley and Steven in Twin Sitters (1995). Christian appeared as his own character on episodes of Empty Nest , Wings and Dream On . Joseph, meanwhile, went it alone as Bobby on another 30 of so episodes of Knots Landing through its 14th-season conclusion in May 1993, then returned for the 1997 reunion movie Knots Landing: Back to the Cul-de-Sac . After acting, Christian worked as an executive in a furniture business and co-owned a CBD business. THR

Cricket subsidiary Sensical plans to refresh the programming monthly, with the possibility of adding additional seasons down the line. Last year, Sesame and Netflix partnered , with PBS stations resuming firstrun broadcasts at the same time they go live on the subscription streamer. A broader expansion strategy, with additional U.S. platforms and international distribution planned for 2027. Sensical, Cricket’s own platform, will also host the channel. Cricket Media, the 50-year-old children’s media company known for its namesake print magazine, acquired majority control of Sensical in February 2025. In the nearly two years since, the company has pursued a diversified strategy as the media landscape and technology continue to evolve. The company has maintained its print presence, but combined it with streaming and newer offerings like the AI product HeyCricket. While the company has made deals with a number of prestige media brands, Sesame Street still represents the pinnacle of kids media. The series “is one of the most trusted and recognizable brands in children’s media, and bringing it to families through free, connected television is an important step in our strategy,” Cricket Media CEO Eric Berger said in a statement. “We’re building a next-generation children’s media company that brings together trusted content and brands, expanded streaming distribution, advertising and new ways for kids to discover and explore content. title: Christian Cousins Dies: Former Child Actor Of ‘Kindergarten Cop’, ‘Knots Landing’ Was 43
full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Christian Cousins Dies: Former Child Actor Of ‘Kindergarten Cop’, ‘Knots Landing’ Was 43 KPop Demon Hunters Announces 2027 Global Arena Tour Dates In North America, U.K. & Europe Michael John Roberts Dies: ‘TripTank’, ‘BoJack Horseman’ Animator, Director & Producer Was 48 View All November 13, 2026 8:14am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Christian Cousins in 2017 and in a 1989 'Knots Landing' publicity photo Facebook/Lorimar Television Christian Cousins , the former child actor who, along with his twin brother Joseph, starred in the 1990 film Arnold Schwarzenegger comedy Kindergarten Cop , died last month following a battle with liver disease. He was 43. His death was announced by his half-brother, Jonas Roeser, on Instagram. “It’s hard to share that my brother, Christian Cousins, has passed away,” Roeser wrote on October 22. “Christian and his twin brother, Joseph ‘Joey’ Cousins, are my brothers through my biological father. They grew up in California while I was in Washington and I didn’t get to know them until I was in college. Before that, I grew up watching them on television in Knots Landing and the lead role of Dominic in Kindergarten Cop with Arnold Schwarzenegger. Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries News Michael John Roberts Dies: ‘TripTank’, ‘BoJack Horseman’ Animator, Director & Producer Was 48 “But those roles are only a small part of how I’ll remember Christian,” Roeser continued. “He was a character, full of passion and energy, with big stories and even bigger dreams. Christian had been very sick with liver disease. It brings me comfort to believe he is now in heaven with his mother, free from the pain he was carrying. Rest easy, Christian. I hope your soul is at rest and that you’ve found peace. You are my brother and you will be missed.” In addition to their Kindergarten Cop role, Christian and twin brother Joseph, who were born March 17, 1983, in Orange County, California, shared the roles of Bobby Gibson Ewing on 88 episodes of CBS’ primetime soap Knots Landing from 1987 to 1993. They also shared roles on Critters 3 (1991) and Eerie, Indiana (1991) and appeared as separate characters on a 1988 episode of Highway to Heaven , a 1989 TV movie called Roxanne: The Prize Pulitzer, Empty Nest (1992) and the film Twin Sitters (1995), their final credit. The young cast of ‘Kindergarten Cop’ with Arnold Schwarzenegger in a 1990 publicity photo Universal/Everett Collection Christian appeared in the 1993 TV movie A Waltons Thanksgiving Reunion as Clay Jones, a son of Judy Norton’s Mary-Ellen Walton character. In a 2020 Kindergarten Cop reunion Zoom hosted by Yahoo Entertainment and featuring the Cousins brothers as well as a surprise appearance by Schwarzenegger, Christian said that, as an adult and having retired from acting, he went into the furniture business as an executive, and also co-owned a CBD business. News of his death was first reported by the New York Post. Cousins is survived by brother Joseph Cousins and half-brother Roeser. Complete survivor information was not immediately available. full_text: × Nov 13, 2026 8:01am PT U2 Gets On Its Boots for First All-New Full-Length Record in Nine Years, ‘Carnaval de Luz,’ With More Callbacks to Band’s ’90s Peaks Than ’80s Glories: Album Review By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest U2 Gets On Its Boots for First All-New Full-Length Record in Nine Years, ‘Carnaval de Luz,’ With More Callbacks to Band’s ’90s Peaks Than ’80s Glories: Album Review 36 minutes ago Taylor Swift to Perform at CMAs for the First Time in 13 Years 2 hours ago ‘Oh, Mary!’ Mania Takes Over L.A.: Director Sam Pinkleton on Bringing the Unruly Broadway Comedy Phenomenon to Full Houses at the Ahmanson 16 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Island “The past and me have got to break up,” Bono sings in the verse that opens “Carnaval de Luz,” U2 ‘s first full-length album of all-new material in nine years. It sounds like a mission statement, doesn’t it? The singer doesn’t linger long on combating nostalgia or breaking out of ingrained patterns, or whatever he means to suggest there. But you can rest assured, if you’ve ever read any U2 interviews this century, that the band is constantly wrestling with its legacy and how to move forward with relevance, just as certainly as Jacob wrestled the angel in “Bullet the Blue Sky.” They have been known to overthink it all, and impatient fans have been known to want to to say: Just put down your pencils and turn in your work, boys! Related Stories 'Love Is Blind' Star Rob Feeley Breaks His Silence on Michaella, the Beekeeper and Why He Nearly Skipped the Reunion 'Blue Eye Samurai' Sets Season 2 Release Date at Netflix It kind of feels like that’s what the band has done with “Carnaval de Luz,” a definitely imperfect but also rewarding and interesting addition to U2’s 46-year catalog. In a “liner notebook” he wrote to accompany the album, Bono quips that “putting the messy in the messianic (is) the job of the frontman.” And there’s messiness aplenty in these 12 songs, which don’t always hang together as easily coherent statements but contain literally hundreds of quotable, fascinating, self-effacingly funny or deeply poetic lines, as if he penned a year’s worth of TED talks about God, the devil, love, ego and our shared humanity and fed them all into a blender. Not that the lyrics are completely random; Spanish phrases abound, and the album is loosely themed around Latin America’s pre-Lent celebrations, just as the two EPs U2 put out earlier this year were tied to Ash Wednesday and Easter. U2 finally figured out how to carve out an album out of all the material they’d amassed by pulling together the songs that best fit a carnaval theme. Suffice it to say, anyway, that as “party albums” go, this is a pretty complicated one, dense in wily aphorisms excavating the realms of philosophy and pop theology. But maybe you don’t want to know about where Bono is in his spiritual quest. You want to know: Does the album rock , in a less radio-conscious or tentative way than some of the albums they were putting out in the 2000s and 2010s? Yes, by and large — and the way in which it rocks is closer to the U2 of the ’90s than an attempt to exactly replicate the signature sounds of the ’80s. One of the hookiest tracks, “La Reina,” gets a little too close to the ’90s for comfort, sounding baldly built on the template of “Even Better Than the Real Thing.” But if that sounds like a step in the right direction of decades to you, there’s a lot to savor in an album that starts with “Go (Carnaval de Luz),” which was purportedly inspired by Suicide but sounds like a punkier version of techno-“Pop,” and ends with a duet with a country legend, “Torn,” with Dolly Parton — in, yes, her last recorded song — taking the place of “Zooropa’s” Johnny Cash. The band is delightfully locked in in this, their 50th anniversary. But the ultimate success of the album will depend on how down you are with Bono at his most unbottled. I groaned a little at “You and me are breaking news / Because the news can’t break us” (in “Superficiality”), but found myself as touched as I was meant to be when Bono speaks up for every human on earth when he sings “No such thing as a small life… / Every life gigantic, huge and romantic / Even greater than it appears” (in “If the World Is at War We Better Not Be”). It’s best to save all the tissues, in any case, for the Dolly duet, which she began writing as a song about a love triangle, before Bono retrofitted it into a ballad about a mother grieved by the division between two warring sons. Captured in the studio just three months shy of being on her deathbed, Parton does some actual belting in the final moments of “Torn,” and Bono is there to meet her, in a flawless blending of voices. Suddenly, thoughts about U2’s relevance seem irrelevant; whether it’s with a final Dolly collab or Bono’s stanza-by-stanza musings, no one does mortal reckonings better. ‘Russell Brand: Open Secret’: Netflix Doc Reveals His ‘Jokes’ About Rape, Making a Girlfriend ‘Brush Her Teeth Until They Bled’ and More ‘La Bola Negra’ Creatives Faced a Ticking Clock to Finish the Film for Cannes, but Waiting for Snow Almost Kept the Ending From Being Shot Latin Grammys Full Winners List: Rosalía Wins Big With Album and Song of the Year Honors ‘Avatar: Seven Havens’ Sets Season 2 Release Date at Paramount+ ‘SVU’ Star Mariska Hargitay Breaks Down Benson and Stabler’s Complicated Reunion and Her Final Choice: ‘There Are So Many Feelings’ Tony Award Winner Lois Smith Joins Colin West’s ‘Outside of Cleveland’: ‘She’s an Icon’ (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments...

title: Kai Cech to Voice Lead in Himalayan Animated Feature ‘Lost in Mandala’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Nov 13, 2026 8:00am PT Kai Cech to Voice Lead in Himalayan Animated Feature ‘Lost in Mandala’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Kai Cech to Voice Lead in Himalayan Animated Feature ‘Lost in Mandala’ (EXCLUSIVE) 49 minutes ago ‘KPop Demon Hunters’ Golden World Tour Sets 2027 Arena Dates 3 hours ago Renny Harlin Launches Harlin House Fellowship for Emerging European Filmmakers, Taps Colin Trevorrow, Tim Miller as Advisors 3 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Incessant Rain Kai Cech , who starred opposite Jack Black in “Dear Santa,” has been cast as the lead voice in “ Lost in Mandala ,” the first animated feature film from Incessant Rain Studios, which is in pre-production. Cech will voice Shanti, a lonely 12-year-old who grew up in an isolated monastery in the Himalayas. Shanti and her friends are accidentally pulled into a magical world concealed inside a sacred mandala. The setting lulls her into a feeling of belonging she has always wanted, but nothing is as it seems. That belonging is shattered and a dark force threatens the world, and returning home means reckoning with the truth of her past and defeating a demon through compassion. Related Stories Maya Jama Strikes Deal With Netflix (EXCLUSIVE) 'Big Mistakes' Season 2 Casts Randall Park, Debi Mazar, T.R. Knight, Jeff Perry “My parents have always emphasized the importance of kindness to all and that my love and empathy for all living things is a superpower,” Cech said. “So this story really struck a chord with me since my character Shanti must find her inner strength through compassion, balance and mindfulness. It’s also a story of friendship and working together to discover who you truly are and what is really important. In addition, I’m just so excited to be a part of Nepal’s first global animated feature film and working with such talented creators.” Kiran Bhakta Joshi created and directs the film. Joshi previously worked as a visual effects supervisor at Disney, with credits on “The Hunchback of Notre Dame,” “The Lion King” and “Beauty and the Beast.” The studio frames the project as a major step for Nepal’s creative sector, combining experience from the global film business with homegrown production capacity. “Growing up in Nepal, I was surrounded by the rich mythology, folklore, and cultural traditions of the Himalayas,” Joshi said. “As a child, I helped create mandalas for traditional ceremonies, fascinated by their beauty without fully understanding their deeper meaning. With ‘Lost in Mandala,’ I want to bring this magical world to life through a story that is culturally rooted yet universally relatable. I’m thrilled to have Kai Cech bring Shanti to life and to collaborate with exceptional storytellers, Zack Stentz, Christopher Jenkins and Richard Chavez, whose creative vision is invaluable in bringing this story to audiences around the world.” Zack Stentz, whose credits include “Thor,” “X-Men: First Class” and Netflix’s “Jurassic World: Camp Cretaceous,” and Christopher Jenkins, whose credits include the Oscar-nominated “Surf’s Up,” “10 Lives” and “Home,” wrote the screenplay. “As a longtime fan of Nepal and its people, I jumped at the opportunity to collaborate with my friend Kiran on ‘Mandala,'” Stentz said. “The result is a love letter to one of the world’s richest yet little-known cultures in the form of a plucky girl and her loyal friends’ adventures in a magical land.” Joshi, Stentz, Jenkins and Nakim Uddin are executive producers, and Deepa Chipalu Joshi produces. Richard Chavez, whose credits include “The Prince of Egypt,” “Mulan” and “Hotel Transylvania,” is production designer. NIBL Equity Partners is a production partner on the film. “Stepping inside the mandala means entering a world where logic bends, geometry comes alive, and the landscape changes with your emotions,” Jenkins said. “In writing Shanti’s adventure, my goal is to create a mind-bending, topsy-turvy odyssey that matches the deep, beautiful spirituality of the Himalayas with a high-stakes fantasy world global audiences have never seen before.” Cech grew up in Northern California and modeled in print for Gap, Old Navy, Mattel and Gymboree before moving into film and television. Her first lead film role, as Gwynn Tan, was in 2022’s “American Girl: Corinne Tan.” She starred with Black in “Dear Santa,” a Paramount holiday comedy, in 2024 and appeared in “Marshmallow,” an independent horror film, in 2025. Osbrink, Paradigm and Brillstein Entertainment Partners represent her. Incessant Rain is an animation, visual effects and game development studio. It makes its own films and games and also provides animation, VFX and production work for international and regional partners. “Lost in Mandala” E.
